mathgap.title: Signed Equality for Difference Statements
mathgap.principle: When a statement equates two differences, treat both sides as signed equations preserving the order of the named variables, i.e., interpret "the number of X that A has more than B equals the difference between C and D" as (A - B) = (C - D).
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a statement uses the pattern "the number of ... that A has more than B is equal to the difference between ... C and D" (or any similar equality of differences).
mathgap.example: Interpreting "Pat has more than Leone equals the difference between Waymon and Lorenzo" as |Pat‑Leone| = Waymon‑Lorenzo or as Pat‑Leone = Waymon (ignoring Lorenzo).

mathgap.title: Iterative Substitution and Propagation
mathgap.principle: Whenever a variable's value becomes known (through a direct count, a solved equation, or a transfer), immediately substitute that value into all pending equations and simplify, repeating until no further substitutions are possible.
mathgap.when_to_apply: After each new piece of information is derived, propagate it throughout the entire system of equations before moving on.
mathgap.example: Solving L = P + 7 but failing to replace L in the equation P - L = W - Lo, leaving the system under‑determined.

mathgap.title: Chronological Evaluation of Comparative Statements
mathgap.principle: Evaluate each comparative statement using the counts as they exist at that point in the text, after applying any earlier transfers, overrides, or direct counts, but before any later changes.
mathgap.when_to_apply: For every comparative statement, refer to the current values of the involved persons at the moment the statement appears.
mathgap.example: Using Waymon's count after the "Eddie gives 33 to Waymon" transfer when evaluating the earlier statement "Pat has more than Leone equals Waymon - Lorenzo".

mathgap.title: Query‑Focused Subsystem Extraction
mathgap.principle: Identify the minimal subset of equations that involve the queried person directly or indirectly, and solve only that subsystem, ignoring unrelated variables.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When the problem asks for a specific person's count, prune the full system to the connected component containing that person before solving.
mathgap.example: Attempting to solve the entire network of 20 variables when only Arleen's count is required, leading to unnecessary complexity and potential mistakes.

mathgap.title: Distinct Name Disambiguation
mathgap.principle: Treat each unique name as a separate variable, even if names differ by only a single character; avoid conflating similar names unless explicitly stated as aliases.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a new name appears in the narrative, ensure it is introduced as a distinct variable.
mathgap.example: Assuming "Leone" and "Leon" refer to the same person and merging their counts.

mathgap.title: Preserve Order in "Difference Between" Phrases
mathgap.principle: When a phrase says "the difference between the number of X that A and B have", interpret it as the signed difference A − B, preserving the order of A and B as written.
mathgap.when_to_apply: For any statement that mentions "difference between ... A and B".
mathgap.example: Interpreting "difference between Waymon and Lorenzo" as Lorenzo − Waymon instead of Waymon − Lorenzo.

mathgap.title: General Comparative Interpretation (more/fewer)
mathgap.principle: Interpret "A has K more than B" as A − B = K, and "A has K fewer than B" as A − B = −K, preserving the direction of the comparison.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a direct comparative statement uses the words "more" or "fewer".
mathgap.example: Interpreting "Leone has 7 more than Pat" as Pat − Leone = 7 (reversing the sign).

mathgap.title: Direct Count Handling with Overrides
mathgap.principle: When a statement says "X has N items", set X's count to N at that point, overriding any previous value for X; later statements (including transfers) may modify X further.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a direct count appears in the narrative.
mathgap.example: Treating "Lorenzo has 15 pineapples" as an immutable initial count, even after a later transfer that changes Lorenzo's total.

mathgap.title: Chronological Transfer Application
mathgap.principle: Apply each transfer statement in the order given, subtracting the specified amount from the giver and adding it to the receiver at that point; subsequent statements see the updated counts.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a transfer appears in the text.
mathgap.example: Ignoring the effect of "Eddie gives 33 to Waymon" when evaluating later statements that involve Waymon, leading to incorrect equations.

mathgap.description: Swapped direction in 'has K more than' statements
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model confuses the subject and object positions in comparative phrasing, reversing the intended sign.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Remember that "A has K more than B" means A's count exceeds B's by K, i.e., A − B = K.

mathgap.why_it_happens: The model defaults to thinking of "difference" as a magnitude, discarding sign information.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Preserve the order and sign: interpret "difference between A and B" as A − B, not |A − B|.

mathgap.description: Ignoring the chronological order of transfers
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model treats transfers as global adjustments rather than point‑in‑time events, applying them after all statements.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Apply each transfer immediately when it appears; earlier statements must use pre‑transfer values, later statements see the updated counts.

mathgap.description: Treating 'has N' as an initial count regardless of position
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model assumes direct counts are immutable base values and does not allow later transfers to modify them.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Set the count at the moment the statement occurs, but allow subsequent transfers or overrides to change it.

mathgap.why_it_happens: The model reads scaling language (e.g., "twice as many") as an additive relation.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Translate multiplicative phrasing into equations (e.g., "A has twice as many as B" becomes A = 2 × B).
